title: Houses in Multiple Occupation
speaker: The Minister for Housing and Planning (Matthew Pennycook)
text: The new national planning policy framework, published on 17 August, includes a more flexible and proportionate policy design to provide greater clarity on the circumstances in which article 4 directions may be appropriate, including where there is an overconcentration of small HMOs. We want to ensure that councils can act properly to regulate HMOs where it is necessary to protect the amenity or wellbeing of an area, and we will continue to keep the powers to regulate HMOs under review.

title: Sporting and Performing Arts Opportunities for Pupils in State Schools
speaker: Baroness Smith of Malvern (Lab)
text: The right reverend Prelate is right that the HAF programme has provided both food and activities for very many children and young people. While we have provided 21 million days to children and young people in England, which have been delivered across 153 local authorities, notwithstanding the £600 million that has been committed to it, we need to look carefully at how we get that to as many children as possible. I cannot commit to changing the entitlement rules but I will take back the points that the right reverend Prelate has made on that programme.

title: Social Housing Bill (Fifth sitting)
speaker: The Chair
text: With this it will be convenient to discuss new clause 63—Provision of electric vehicle charging points in new social housing developments— “(1) Within six months of the passing of this Act, the Secretary of State must, by regulations made by statutory instrument, make provision to require new social housing developments to include electric vehicle charging points. (2) A statutory instrument containing regulations under this section may not be made unless a draft of the instrument has been laid before and approved by a resolution of each House of Parliament.”

title: Binance Security Breach: Consumer Exposure and Interim Safeguards
speaker: The Earl of Kinnoull (CB)
text: My Lords, North Korea has form in attacking financial markets to fund its foreign currency requirements. It attacked the London reinsurance markets 15 years or so ago, when there were heavy losses for London reinsurers and losses for German reinsurers. This is a pattern of attack by North Korea. Can the Minister tell us whether we are co-operating internationally, not just with the Americans but with the Germans in this instance, to try to make sure that we can stamp out this abuse by North Korea?

title: Impact of Defence Spending
speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Wales (Anna McMorrin)
text: This Government are delivering the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the cold war by investing £298 billion over the next four years to strengthen our national security and keep us safe. Wales is well placed to benefit from this investment, with 20,000 defence jobs already in Wales. Every pound that we invest in defence should be judged by what it does. We want to ensure that all investment brings jobs and skills, and strengthens our national security.

title: Representation of the People Bill
speaker: Lord Wallace of Saltaire (LD)
text: I apologise; it is rather eccentric. The Parliament Choir is performing this evening, and the dress rehearsal starts at 4 pm—I have said that I will be late. I add that there is strong scientific evidence that collective singing in schools improves social cohesion and concentration. I am not sure that the last Government accepted that scientific evidence—they did not act on it. But if we are talking about scientific evidence in schools, singing matters as well.

title: Reservoirs and Water Supplies
speaker: Lord Roborough (Con)
text: My Lords, the concerning levels of water in storage—17% beneath seasonal norms, as the Minister mentioned—reflects not just a dry year but systematic underinvestment by the water industry against long-standing forecasts for demand growth and climate change. What assessment have the Government made of the speed, cost and volume of improvement that is possible from nature-based solutions and on-farm reservoirs, versus the expense, controversy and long timelines of new reservoirs? I declare my interest as a farmer and landowner.

title: Financial Services and Markets Bill [Lords]
speaker: Dame Meg Hillier
text: It is worth noting that, in the end, there were two redundancies as a result of the merger, all the backroom costs were the same and the only thing that will change, when the legislation finally goes through, is that the board will go, which is a saving of about £100,000.

title: Automobile Industry: ZEV Mandate
speaker: Baroness in Waiting/Government Whip (Baroness Dacres of Lewisham) (Lab)
text: The automotive sector’s future is zero emissions. The Government are investing more than £7.5 billion to drive investments and safeguard jobs for the future. Tata is investing £4 billion in the UK gigafactory, with further investments from Stellantis, Nissan, Bentley, McLaren and others. We are taking a balanced approach to the transition. We have just closed a consultation reviewing the ZEV mandate. We are working with the devolved Governments to publish the outcome as soon as possible.

title: Rosebank Oilfield: Government Policy
speaker: Olivia Blake
text: Between 21 and 28 June this year—just eight days—there were 2,124 heat-associated deaths, which is 620 more deaths in one week alone than in the whole summer of 2025. How many health risks or deaths are needed before the Opposition get back around the table and rejoin the consensus that action on climate is not only critical, but necessary, and not a nice-to-have?

title: Drugs: Prohibition and Criminalisation
speaker: Lord Hanson of Flint (Lab)
text: I am grateful for my noble friend’s question. The use of drug courts, and judges having ownership of individuals who go through those courts and of the treatment those individuals get, is extremely important. That is a matter for the Ministry of Justice, but it is certainly something we are encouraging. We have put in place, as we did during previous Labour Governments up to 2010, significant numbers of drug treatment orders, which focus on helping people get off drugs in the first place.

title: Grassroots Sports: Facilities for Girls
speaker: Nick Smith (Blaenau Gwent and Rhymney) (Lab)
text: Will the Secretary of State please join me in thanking the volunteers at Junior Parkrun at Parc Bryn Bach in Tredegar. It has good facilities, but their hard work has doubled the number of girls and boys getting out to run on a Sunday morning. Having said that, research from Sky shows that girls in my constituency still do an hour and 16 minutes less sport each week than boys. Can she give us the wider picture of the steps that she is taking to close that gap and get more girls to be active?

title: British Steel: Nationalisation
speaker: Lord Fox (LD)
text: I thank the Minister for that Answer. This Question is about day-to-day operational costs. In March this year, the National Audit Office put those costs to the taxpayer at £1.3 million a day. What are the financial targets that we, the shareholders, are putting on British Steel? We want British Steel to succeed, but it needs to perform better to do that. It is good that the management is planning ahead, but what is it doing operationally, day to day, to drive down costs?

title: Homes and Planning Bill
speaker: Sam Carling (North West Cambridgeshire) (Lab)
text: It is great to hear about the good work that my hon. Friend’s council is doing through its local plan. I have two local planning authorities in my constituency, Labour-run Peterborough and Lib Dem-run Huntingdonshire. In Labour-run Peterborough, the new affordable housing requirements in the emerging local plan specify that 30% of homes must be affordable housing, of which 30% needs to be for social rent. Will my hon. Friend join me in calling on Huntingdonshire, under the Liberal Democrats, to do something similar? Right now, its affordable housing requirements do not set aside anything for social rent.

title: Point of Order: Rectification Procedure
speaker: Sammy Wilson (East Antrim) (DUP)
text: On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I wish to apologise to the House for my failure to declare an interest when participating in a Westminster Hall debate on 22 June 2026 on the topic of pro-Israel influence on UK politics and democracy. When I spoke during the debate, I inadvertently failed to declare a relevant interest, which is that I visited Israel between 23 and 30 October on a trip funded by the embassy of Israel. This was in breach of the rules and I apologise to the House for that error.

title: Drone Attack Risks
speaker: Lord Hanson of Flint (Lab)
text: The noble and gallant Lord makes an extremely important point. In the defence investment plan, which is obviously a Ministry of Defence capability, we have supported £750 million for counterdrone capabilities, and as I mentioned to the noble Lord, Lord Farmer, a further £470 million to enhance military site security. But it is absolutely right that we need to have intelligence-led operations that ensure we know when any potential hostile actor is trying to undertake activity and that we continually keep under review our skills, capability and resilience. That is an important point not just for the Home Office but also for the MoD.

title: Oil-fired Heating
speaker: Torcuil Crichton (Na h-Eileanan an Iar) (Lab)
text: In Scotland, the SNP Government run the heating oil fund centrally, but despite boasting that they would double the fund to £10 million, only 7,028 households out of 169,000 in Scotland that rely on heating oil have had approval from the heating oil fund. Of over 12,000 households in my constituency, half of which use heating oil, only 324 have been able to claim the £300. Will the Minister meet Scottish Ministers and urge them to get that money out the door, take the rurality and insularity of islands into account, and widen the eligibility so that more people can get support?

title: Parking (Code of Practice) Act 2019
speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds (Lab)
text: That is an interesting reflection, but, quite honestly, given the history of where we have been on this journey, the most important thing is that we do it accurately so that it is not subject to challenge. We live in a very litigious environment, as we know, and parking is the No. 1 area in that. Let us make sure that we get it right, but also do everything we can to expedite the changes and bring them into force as soon as we can.

title: Community Hospitals and Step-down Care
speaker: Liz Saville Roberts
text: It behoves me to point out the obvious, which is that these are all matters to be answered by a Health Minister in Wales, and that the Health Minister here cannot answer them. I also need to point out that an extra £500 million was allocated to health in Wales in yesterday’s Welsh budget. It includes a national clinical plan in the spring and a community shift of expenditure directed to health boards of 0.5% of their budgets towards community services.

title: Land Use Framework
speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering (Con)
text: My Lords, given that 10% of productive farmland is going to be taken out of production under the land use framework, will the Minister explain the thinking behind the department giving a grant of almost £2 million for the acquisition of the Rothbury estate for rewilding—so not for food production at all?

title: El Niño: National Resilience
speaker: Dan Jarvis
text: I am grateful to my hon. Friend for making those points. Let me say to him that we are taking action to make the UK the most resilient country that it can be, including in the face of our changing climate. That includes investing in nine new reservoirs across the country, more than 600 flood defence projects across England and £2.6 billion to climate-proof rail infrastructure and keep the UK moving. All of this makes us more resilient and contributes to our vital role as a dependable ally.

title: Access to Clinical Trials
speaker: Baroness Pidgeon (LD)
text: The Government have made welcome progress in speeding up commercial clinical trials, but over 95% of patients take part in non-commercial interventional trials, often funded by charities. Cancer Research UK expects 80,000 people to participate in its trials over the next five years, so what steps will the Government take to speed up these types of trials to help find treatments for rarer conditions?

title: Complications from Abortions (Annual Report) Bill [HL]
speaker: Baroness Merron (Lab)
text: Yes; my interpretation is clearly somewhat different from the noble Lord’s. I finish by saying that work is continuing to clear the backlog, which we know is the case, and to catch up on the publication of the annual abortion statistics reports. Dates for the publication of the 2025 and 2026 annual official abortion statistics will be announced in due course. On the point that the noble Lord, Lord Kamall, made about communication and contact with pharma companies, I would be pleased to write to him further on that.

title: Finance Bill
speaker: Graham Stuart
text: I am extremely grateful to the Chairman of the Treasury Committee for giving way. I think it may have been to her Committee that Helen Miller of the Institute for Fiscal Studies pointed out that not one of the 98 measures in this Budget had a positive growth score, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility. Could she comment on that feature of this enormous yet non-growth-producing Budget?

title: Health Bill
speaker: Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge (Con)
text: The Minister’s response is the same as that which the Government gave to my question in March 2025. She referred to the need for a consultation. Did that consultation begin 20 months ago, when we first raised the issue? The Minister reassured us then that the Government were “considering … the priorities”, including the roles that digital clinics play, “should an opportunity for legislative reform arise”.—[Official Report, 12/3/25; col. 699.] That is a direct quote from 20 months ago. Has that consultation begun?

title: Second Scottish Independence Referendum
speaker: Pete Wishart
text: I am not giving way. We owe it to those who oppose independence just as much as we do to those who support it. Support for independence currently sits a little bit north of 50%. Over 50% of the people in Scotland want to see an independent nation.

title: Representation of the People Bill
speaker: Lord Jackson of Peterborough (Con)
text: If the Government are not minded to accept the noble Lord’s Amendment 111, I propose a potential halfway house: secondary legislation to encourage local authorities particularly and electoral returning officers to have at least a consistent presentation of the data, so that we can see turnout by ward and how many candidates or spoiled ballot papers there were in every local authority—whether it be district council, county council or borough council—across the whole country with a consistent format. This is the pattern in other countries.

title: Restoration and Renewal of the Palace of Westminster
speaker: Marie Goldman (Chelmsford) (LD)
text: I wonder whether the right hon. Gentleman would like to check his figures. He just said that Notre-Dame has a quarter of the footprint of the Palace of Westminster. I believe Notre-Dame to have a floorspace of 5% of the Palace of Westminster, making it one twentieth of the size. Would he like to correct the record?

title: Technical Education: Secondary Schools
speaker: Lord Wallace of Saltaire (LD)
text: My Lords, what is the role of FE colleges in all this? I declare an interest: Shipley College is based in Saltaire. I am very conscious that a lot of 16 to 18 year-olds who would otherwise drop out of education do technical courses in FE colleges. How are the Government going to make sure that these play a very worthwhile role in developing this further?

title: Small and Medium-sized Enterprises
speaker: The Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (Jonathan Reynolds)
text: As official statistics show, despite considerable pressure arising from international events, British businesses continue to be resilient, and growth to the end of the year in September was back to over 2%. Small and medium-sized enterprises represent 99% of businesses in the UK, and they are the backbone of that resilience and success. The Department supports them in a number of ways, including increased access to finance, cutting regulation, increasing small business rates relief thresholds, and tackling late payments with the Commercial Payments Bill.

title: AI systems: NHS Data
speaker: The Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State, Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (Baroness Lloyd of Effra) (Lab)
text: My Lords, AI developers should keep their systems under safe control. We expect prompt, transparent reporting of unexpected behaviour. In respect of breach of systems, the Computer Misuse Act applies to AI developers, and they must not breach systems. If breaches happen, victims should be informed immediately. If personal data, such as NHS records, is accessed, the Information Commission should be informed within 72 hours. The cyber Bill strengthens protections for essential services such as NHS trusts. Regulated AI services must report significant loss of control incidents within 24 hours.

title: Other Correction
speaker: Steve Darling
text: When the disability living allowance transitioned into PIP, 600 deaths, most of which were suicides, were linked to the DWP. What lessons have been learned from that, and what action will the Secretary of State take following the Timms review? [Official Report, 23 November 2026; Vol. 794, c. 17.] Written correction submitted by the hon. Member for Torbay (Steve Darling):
